title: Data Intensive Physics - Project Notes
text:
Preface
This is the repository for my coursework project for Data Intensive Physics (unit code PHYSM0070) during my final year at the University of Bristol.
This project is working on using machine learning to identify anomalies in the Euclid Q1 dataset. This work has made use of the Euclid Q1 data from the Euclid mission of the European Space Agency (ESA), 2025, https://doi.org/10.57780/esa-2853f3b  [1]  [2]  [3]  [4]  [5]  [6]  [7]
This is a Quarto book.
To learn more about Quarto books visit https://quarto.org/docs/books.

Note




The SPE_WIDE-CAT-MOD file contains four tables:

Catalogue: All spectral lines with: [ID, the central wavelength, the name of the line, the type (absorb or emit)]
Galaxy models: The parameters for a galaxy spectral model for each galaxy candidate
Star models: The parameters for a star spectral model for each star candidate
QSO models: The parameters for a QSO spectral model for each QSO candidate

The SPE_WIDE-CAT-LIN file contains four tables:

The spectral line measurements
Measurement of absorption atomic indices
Measurement of absorption molecular indices
Continuum features

The EUC_SPE_WIDE-CAT-Z file contains five tables:

Quality flags
Classification information
Up to 5 redshift candidates for galaxy
1 relative velocity candidate for star
up to 5 redshift candidates for QSO

1.2 Discoveries Within the Data Structure

1.2.1 Spectral Energy Distributions
The STARSED and GALAXYSED files contain spectral energy distributions of the objects if the object can be classified as either object. Of the 111422 objects:

1963 have a stellar SED (1.8% of total)
57919 have a galactic SED (52.0% of total)
1963 have both a stellar and galactic SED

An interesting feature of this is that every object that has an SED for a stellar classification also has an SED for a galactic classification. An example of one such object is shown below.

title: 2  Research on ML Anomaly Detection
text:
Anomaly detection split into 3 methods based on label availability:

Supervised detection

Training accomplished with a “coaching” set of tagged examples of anomaly/normal
Unknown data can then be shown to the model and categorised

Semi-supervised

Assume training set consists entirely of tagged examples
Doesn’t require labels for unusual datapoints, only those in known categories
e.g. using a deep auto encoder?

Unsupervised

Function unattended without need for training data
Assumes common occurrences outnumber anomalies by factor 10


Outcome of detection can either be scores or labels

Score would allow the analyst to select the most anomalous objects

Techniques

Classification

Will be supervised
Algorithm to classify between anomalous and non-anomalous data
Classification Tree

AKA call tree or prediction model
Flow chart structure

Naive Bayes Network

Mathematical correlations or links between variables
More effective than decision tree for large data
See  [2] for example

Neural Network

Clustering

K-Means

Useful for unlabelled data
Anomalies can be found by looking at distance from centroid

Expectation maximisation

Allocating a datapoint to a group based on the cluster mean
Datapoints assigned weights based on likelihood of participation in the group

Outlier detection

Finding anomalies which do not follow a trend
Distance based approach
Density based approach (denser section regarded as normal, thin part not)


Cascading

Different methods can be cascaded to take advantage of the benefits of multiple

title: 3  Project Plan
text:
3.1.1 Summary [From Here]
Isolation forest works as follows:

Random partitioning

The algorithm selects a random feature from the dataset
The data is split at a random value dividing it in two
This is repeated to create binary trees

Isolation path

This is the number of splits required
Anomalies have shorter paths as they differ more

Ensemble of trees

Builds a group of trees
Each is created independently
Gives diverse isolation paths for each datapoint
Ensures robustness and reliability

Anomaly scoring

Anomalies are scored by averaging the path lengths across the trees
Shorter path lengths are more anomalous

Classification

A threshold on the anomaly score classifies datapoints as normal or anomalous
Points above the threshold are anomalies


This method is highly efficient and scalable
